6._section_summary: This introduction discusses the increasing global prevalence of negative body image and eating disorders, moving beyond their traditional view as culture-bound syndromes. It highlights the role of modernization, urbanization, and globalization in promoting a thin ideal, and the impact of transmigration on body image, particularly for non-Western migrants. The present study (Study X) focuses on Zimbabwean women, comparing body image (operationalized as actual-ideal weight discrepancy and body appreciation) between those in Zimbabwe and those in Britain, hypothesizing more negative body image among the latter.

The study used the BAS, which did not reduce factorially to one dimension in this non-Western sample. It also found that greater exposure to Western media was associated with lower body appreciation in both samples. The study, referred to as 'this study', involved two distinct samples: Zimbabwean women in Zimbabwe and Zimbabwean migrant women in Britain.

3._section_summary: This section details the participants for the study, which includes two distinct samples of Zimbabwean women. The first sample consists of 140 women from the community in Harare, Zimbabwe, with a mean age of 25.34 years and a mean self-reported BMI of 24.81. 4._section_summary: This section details the exploratory factor analyses of Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) data for two distinct subgroups: a migrant sample and a non-migrant sample. For both samples, factor analyses revealed two factors, with a General Body Appreciation factor consistently emerging. The non-migrant sample showed significantly higher general body appreciation than the migrant sample.

5.evidence_source: Our results also showed that the BAS did not reduce factorially to one dimension, as has been found among Western samples (Avalos et al., 2005); rather, there was one dominant factor related to general body appreciation, which is consistent with work conducted among other non-Western samples (Swami, Campana, et al., 2011; Swami & Chamorro-Premuzic, 2008).
5._section_summary: This discussion section compares body image and appreciation between Zimbabwean migrants in Britain and their counterparts in Zimbabwe, finding that migrants had more negative body image and greater weight discrepancy. The study used the BAS, which did not reduce factorially to one dimension in this non-Western sample. It also found that greater exposure to Western media was associated with lower body appreciation in both samples. The study, referred to as 'this study', involved two distinct samples: Zimbabwean women in Zimbabwe and Zimbabwean migrant women in Britain.
